summary: Explains how IETF protocols should use Ethernet frame formats and IEEE 802 parameters, and sets IANA rules for handing out values under the IANA Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI). It also provides values meant for use in documentation. It replaces RFC 7042, and is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Every network card has a name tag from a maker. This document says how the IETF borrows those tag rules, who hands out new ones, and which pretend tags are safe to use in examples.

questions: what mac addresses are for documentation
subtitle: How IETF protocols use Ethernet and IEEE 802 identifiers, how IANA hands out values under its own OUI, and which addresses are safe for examples.

tldr.problem: IETF protocols rely on MAC addresses, EtherTypes and other IEEE 802 identifiers, but IANA needs clear rules for assigning values under its own Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI) and documents need safe example values.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains the structure of MAC identifiers, sets requirements and Expert Review or IESG Ratification procedures for assignments under the IANA OUI 00-00-5E, and reserves blocks of addresses and protocol numbers for documentation.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 7042 as the BCP on the topic, creates no new IANA registries and changes no existing assignment.

today: RFC 9542 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 141) and obsoletes RFC 7042. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it in the metadata for this site.

sections.title: Purpose and the IEEE Registration Authority
sections.content:
Some IETF protocols use Ethernet frame formats and IEEE 802 parameters such as Media Access Control (MAC) addresses and protocol identifiers. The IEEE Registration Authority manages these identifiers, sometimes assigning blocks whose sub-assignment is managed by the block's owner. It has been the registration authority for Ethernet parameters since 1986; the job was originally Xerox's.

The IEEE RA assigned IANA the Organizationally Unique Identifier 00-00-5E. This document sets the IANA rules for code points under that OUI, including MAC addresses and protocol identifiers, and provides values for documentation. Its descriptions of IANA policy are authoritative, while its descriptions of IEEE policy are only informative.

The document uses the term IESG Ratification for a combination of Expert Review and IESG Approval from RFC 8126, where IESG Approval is needed only if the Expert does not reject the request.
sections.eli5: A big group called the IEEE gives out name tags for network cards. The Internet's record-keeper, IANA, got its own batch of tags and this document says how it shares them out.

sections.title: MAC Identifiers and the IANA Block
sections.content:
A 48-bit MAC address that is globally unique is also called an EUI-48. It starts with a prefix assigned by the IEEE RA, followed by bits the prefix owner assigns. Three prefix lengths exist as of 2024: 24 bits (MA-L), 28 bits (MA-M) and 36 bits (MA-S), leaving the owner 24, 20 and 12 bits respectively.

Special bits sit at the bottom of the first octet. The M bit marks group (multicast or broadcast) addresses when it is one. The X bit is the universal/local bit: zero means a global address controlled by the prefix owner. When X is one and the IEEE 802 Structured Local Address Plan (SLAP) is in effect, the Y and Z bits split local space into four quadrants: Administratively Assigned, Extended Local, Reserved and Standard Assigned. A CID is a 24-bit Company Identifier for organizations that need an identifier but not subsidiary global addresses.

Under the IANA OUI there are 224 unicast identifiers from 00-00-5E-00-00-00 and 224 multicast identifiers from 01-00-5E-00-00-00. Sub-blocks include VRRP and IPv6 VRRP unicast blocks, 223 multicast addresses for IPv4 multicast, and 220 for MPLS multicast.
sections.eli5: A network address is like a home address that starts with the street name, and the street owner picks the house numbers. A few special switches at the start say whether it is for one house or a whole group of houses.

sections.title: 64-Bit Identifiers and Other IETF Uses
sections.content:
IEEE also defines 64-bit identifiers (EUI-64), used in IEEE 1394, IEEE 802.15.4 and InfiniBand. IETF used a Modified EUI-64, which inverts the X bit, to form the lower 64 bits of some IPv6 addresses. That method is now deprecated and RFC 8064 is recommended instead. Under the IANA OUI, an EUI-48 can become a Modified EUI-64 by inserting FF-FE in the middle, and the block 02-00-5E-FE-xx-xx-xx-xx is reserved for holders of IPv4 addresses.

The IETF also uses two other 48-bit ranges. Multicast identifiers starting 33-33 serve IPv6 multicast per RFC 2464. The CF series (CF-00-00 through CF-FF-FF), created by RFC 2153 for software vendors, was deprecated by RFC 5342 and IANA was told to assign no more.

For CBOR, IANA assigned tag 48 for a MAC address (an octet string whose length shows 48 or 64 bits) and tag 1048 for an OUI or CID (an octet string of length 3).
sections.eli5: There are also longer name tags, and some old ways of building them are no longer recommended. Two special prefixes were set aside for particular jobs like IPv6 group messages.

sections.title: Ethernet Protocol Parameters
sections.content:
Near the start of a frame, a protocol identifier says what the frame contains. There are two kinds. EtherTypes are 16-bit values, equal to or larger than 0x0600, placed right after the destination and source MAC addresses. LSAPs are 8-bit identifiers that come in a pair (DSAP and SSAP) after a length field, which must be below 0x5DD so it is not mistaken for an EtherType. This style is called LLC.

Neither kind is assigned by IANA; the IEEE RA assigns them. But both can carry five-octet protocol identifiers under an OUI. In the SNAP format this looks like xx-xx-AA-AA-03-yy-yy-yy-zz-zz, and with the OUI Extended EtherType 0x88B7 it looks like 88-B7-yy-yy-yy-zz-zz.

Two-octet protocol numbers under the IANA OUI take the form 88-B7-00-00-5E-qq-qq. New assignments must be for standards use, include a version field or equivalent marking, be documented in an Internet-Draft or RFC, and not duplicate a protocol that has an EtherType. Protocol number 0x0042 is for documentation.
sections.eli5: A frame starts with a label saying what is inside, like writing LETTER or PARCEL on an envelope. Some labels come from the IEEE, and IANA can make labels of its own using its own prefix.

sections.title: Assignment Rules and Procedure
sections.content:
Assignments of 48-bit or 64-bit blocks under the IANA OUI must be for standards purposes, be a power-of-two-sized block starting at a matching boundary, not be used to evade vendors' need to get their own IEEE block, and be documented in an Internet-Draft or RFC. Small and medium 48-bit blocks (up to 216 identifiers) need Expert Review; blocks of 217 or more need IESG Ratification. For 64-bit identifiers the dividing line is 228 versus 229. Reserved values also need IESG Ratification.

The applicant fills in a template from Appendix A and sends it to IANA, which forwards it to an appointed Expert. A disapproval from the Expert means denial. For IESG Ratification, if the Expert favors the request or is uncertain, IANA forwards it to the IESG, which must decide whether to grant it.

IANA should request an additional OUI from the IEEE RA when either multicast or unicast space under 00-00-5E is 90% or more exhausted.
sections.eli5: To get a batch of tags you fill in a form. A helper checks small requests quickly, and for very large or special requests a bigger committee must also agree.

sections.title: Documentation Values
sections.content:
Using designated documentation values reduces the chance of conflicts with deployed code points. The RFC assigns these 48-bit blocks: unicast 00-00-5E-00-53-00 through 00-00-5E-00-53-FF and multicast 01-00-5E-90-10-00 through 01-00-5E-90-10-FF. It also lists documentation blocks for 64-bit addresses, some derived from the IPv4 documentation addresses. The documentation protocol number is 0x0042 under the IANA OUI.

The same example value, 0x42, is the documentation specifier for other OUI-based parameters, and value 42 in the LLDP TLV subtypes registry is an example for use in documentation.
sections.eli5: When you write an example, use these pretend tags. Then nobody accidentally copies a real person's tag into their computer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document is not directly concerned with security, apart from a few points. Documentation-only addresses can end up coded and released, or conflict with later real use, and reserving dedicated values reduces that risk. MAC addresses can be configured and spoofed, so networks should be cautious using them to enforce policy. They also identify an interface and can be used to track a device and its users; the RFC points to MAC address randomization as a partial mitigation.
sections.eli5: A name tag can be faked, so do not trust it too much. It can also be used to follow a device around.

fields.name: EtherType
fields.desc: At least 0x0600; says what the protocol data is.
